title: Circadian tumor infiltration and function of CD8+ T cells dictate immunotherapy efficacy
one_line: Mouse melanoma work showing that tumor-infiltrating leukocyte numbers and CD8+ T cell phenotype oscillate across the day under endothelial-clock control, so evening-timed CAR T and anti-PD-1 dosing works better.
key_claims: Tumor-infiltrating leukocyte numbers in mouse melanoma oscillate diurnally, peaking in the evening.
The rhythm is driven by the circadian clock in tumor endothelial cells via rhythmic ICAM-1 adhesion molecule expression.
TIL phenotype as well as number oscillates, with a more anti-tumorigenic profile in the evening and PD-1 on CD8+ T cells peaking in the morning, trough in the evening.
Timed CAR T-cell and anti-PD-1 administration in mice was more effective given in the evening, matching peak infiltration and favorable phenotype.

In human melanoma samples TIL number and exhausted:non-exhausted CD8+ ratio varied by time of day (favorable state predicted in the morning), and higher expression of the mouse evening T cell signature correlated with better checkpoint blockade response.
limitations: Work centers on melanoma models, so generalization to other tumor types is untested (authors' stated limitation).
Molecular mechanisms behind the observed oscillations remain incompletely defined (authors' stated limitation).
Optimal human dosing time is inferred from correlative samples and signatures, not from a prospective randomized trial.
Mouse evening optimum versus human morning prediction reflects species phase differences that are not directly validated clinically.
Circadian regulation of non-CD8 immune populations in the tumor microenvironment is not resolved.
open_questions: Do prospective randomized chronotherapy trials of anti-PD-1 or CAR T show an outcome benefit from time-of-day dosing in humans?
Does endothelial clock or ICAM-1 disruption abolish both the infiltration rhythm and the timing-dependent therapy benefit?
Do the same rhythms hold in non-melanoma tumors and in patients with disrupted or shifted circadian phase?
